summary: An AVL tree is a binary search tree that keeps itself balanced: for every node the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Rotations after inserts and deletes restore the invariant, guaranteeing O(log n) search, insert, and delete.

sections.heading: Balance factor
sections.body: balance(node) = height(left) - height(right). In an AVL tree every node has balance -1, 0, or +1. Each node stores its height so balance is O(1) to compute. An AVL tree of n nodes has height at most about 1.44 log2(n).

sections.heading: Rotations
sections.body: A rotation is a local pointer rearrangement that changes heights but preserves BST order.

sections.heading: The four imbalance cases
sections.body: After inserting, walk back up. At the first node z with |balance| = 2:
bullets: Left-Left (balance > 1, new key in left child's left): rotate right at z.
Right-Right (balance < -1, key in right child's right): rotate left at z.
Left-Right (balance > 1, key in left child's right): rotate left at the left child, then right at z.
Right-Left (balance < -1, key in right child's left): rotate right at the right child, then left at z.

sections.heading: Insertion
sections.body: Insert as in a normal BST, then recompute heights on the way back up and rebalance.

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Search, insert, delete: O(log n) worst case.
An insertion needs at most one single or double rotation.
A deletion may need O(log n) rotations along the path.
Space: O(n), plus a height field per node.

sections.body: Delete like a BST (replace a two-child node by its in-order successor), then rebalance every ancestor on the way up. Unlike insertion, one fix may not be enough because the subtree height can shrink and propagate upward.

bullets: AVL is more strictly balanced: faster lookups, slower inserts/deletes (more rotations).
Red-black trees allow a looser height (up to 2 log n) with fewer rotations; used in std::map, TreeMap, and the Linux scheduler.
Choose AVL for read-heavy workloads, red-black for write-heavy ones.

sections.body: A plain BST fed 1, 2, 3, ... becomes a linked list with O(n) operations. An AVL tree rotates at each step and stays near log n height, so sorted input is safe.
Check three invariants after each operation: BST ordering via inorder traversal, stored heights equal the recomputed heights, and every balance factor lies in [-1, 1].

bullets: Real-time systems needing predictable lookup time.
Order statistics when augmented with subtree sizes.
Interval and range queries when augmented.

takeaways: Balance factor must stay in {-1, 0, +1} at every node.
Fix imbalance with single (LL, RR) or double (LR, RL) rotations.
Guarantees O(log n) search, insert, delete.
More strictly balanced than red-black trees: faster reads, costlier updates.
